reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autoimmune blistering disorder triggered by drugs, most classically thiol-containing agents such as penicillamine and captopril
Non-thiol drugs (including some antibiotics and other ACE inhibitors) can also induce it, often with a picture resembling idiopathic pemphigus
Presents with flaccid blisters and erosions of skin and sometimes mucosae, with a pemphigus foliaceus-like pattern being common with thiol drugs
A positive Nikolsky sign (shearing of the epidermis with lateral pressure) reflects loss of keratinocyte adhesion
Histology shows intraepidermal acantholysis, and direct immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular IgG deposition
Circulating antibodies target desmoglein 1 and/or desmoglein 3, as in idiopathic pemphigus
Thiol-induced cases often remit after drug withdrawal, whereas non-thiol-induced disease may behave more like classical pemphigus and require immunosuppression
The cornerstone of management is identifying and withdrawing the culprit drug, with corticosteroids or immunosuppressants for persistent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Drug-induced pemphigus involves loss of adhesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis) mediated by autoantibodies against the desmosomal proteins desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3. Thiol-containing drugs such as penicillamine are thought to interact directly with sulphydryl groups in the desmoglein molecules or in the enzymes maintaining desmosomal integrity, disrupting cell-cell adhesion and, in some patients, provoking a true autoantibody response. Non-thiol drugs may act as haptens or otherwise trigger an autoimmune reaction that more closely mirrors idiopathic pemphigus. The result is intraepidermal blistering with flaccid bullae and erosions. Because part of the mechanism can be biochemical rather than purely immune, thiol-induced disease frequently resolves once the drug is cleared, whereas antibody-driven non-thiol cases can persist.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous pemphigoid and other subepidermal blistering diseases
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histology showing intraepidermal acantholysis
Direct immunofluorescence for intercellular IgG and C3 deposition
Indirect immunofluorescence and desmoglein 1 and 3 antibody assays
Detailed drug history focusing on thiol and other implicated agents
Screening for underlying malignancy where paraneoplastic disease is possible
redFlags: Extensive skin denudation with risk of fluid loss and secondary infection
Significant mucosal involvement impairing intake or airway
Rapidly progressive blistering despite drug withdrawal
reference.prognosis: Thiol-induced pemphigus often remits within weeks to months of stopping the drug, whereas non-thiol-induced disease may persist and require ongoing immunosuppression. Overall prognosis is generally better than idiopathic pemphigus when the trigger is identified and removed early.
pitfalls: Failing to review the medication list and missing the causative drug
Assuming all cases resolve on withdrawal, when non-thiol-induced disease may need immunosuppression
Mistaking it for idiopathic pemphigus and not stopping the trigger
Overlooking mucosal disease and its complications
management: Withdraw the triggering drug, particularly thiol agents such as penicillamine and captopril, which frequently leads to remission without further treatment
For persistent disease, especially non-thiol-induced, give systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil
Use rituximab for refractory or severe disease, as in idiopathic pemphigus
Provide supportive skin and erosion care and attentive oral and mucosal hygiene where mucosae are involved
Monitor clinical activity and desmoglein 1 and 3 antibody titres to guide tapering of immunosuppression
Screen for underlying malignancy where paraneoplastic pemphigus is possible, and manage under dermatology
